lessons.title: Food and drink: the object (what you eat)
lessons.goal: Name food and drink, say what you eat and drink and ask someone else.

grammar.point: A verb like essen or trinken can have an object: the thing you eat or drink. It comes after the verb: Ich esse Brot.
grammar.oneLine: Ich esse Brot. Verb in part 2, the thing you eat after it.

mistake.why: Only du and er/sie say isst. ich takes esse.

terms.meaning: the thing the verb works on: the thing you eat, drink, buy or have
the person who does the verb
a word like was (what) that starts a W-question

cards.title: Before we start: food and drink
cards.body: You are hungry and a friend asks: What do you eat? Chapter 4 is about food: eating, ordering, shopping and offering. Today you name what you eat or drink with one new idea: the object.
steps: You already know: Ich spiele … and the verb in part 2
New today: the object, the thing you eat or drink
By the end you can: say Ich esse Brot and ask Was isst du?

examples.why: New today: Brot is the object, the thing you eat.
New today: the thing comes after the verb.

cards.more: Picture a sentence as a tiny story. Someone does something, and something is on the receiving end. Ben drinks water: Ben is the one who acts, the water is the thing that gets drunk. That thing is called the object. In German it simply comes after the verb, like in English. Nothing scary! You will meet it in small steps in the next cards.

cards.title: The object: what you eat or drink
cards.body: Some verbs need a thing to work on. Who eats? Ich. That is the subject. What do I eat? Brot. That is the object. The object answers the question: what?
cards.more: Think of a sandwich shop. You order: I eat a roll. The roll is the thing that gets eaten, so it is the object. Every eat-or-drink sentence has this little pattern: someone, the verb, and then a thing. English works in exactly the same order, so you can lean on it. Step 1: find the verb. Step 2: ask who? That is the subject. Step 3: ask what? That is the object. Extra example: Leon isst Käse. Käse is the object.
cards.lead: This lesson starts with food and drink. On this card: the object, the thing that gets eaten or drunk and answers the question what, so you can say what you have on your plate.

deeper.text: Here is a trick to find the object: say the verb, then ask was? The word that answers is the object. Notice that food words often come with no article at all when you mean food in general, like Brot or Wasser. English does the same: I eat bread, not I eat the bread.

cards.title: Food words: learn the article too
cards.body: Every food word has a gender: der, die or das. Learn the article with the word. In the next lessons the article can change, so you must know it. Das ist … names a thing.
cards.more: Think of a name tag on every food. The tag says der, die or das. You cannot see the tag from the shape of the food, so you learn it together with the word, like a first name and a last name. Step 1: say der Apfel, never just Apfel. Step 2: say it three times. Extra example: der Saft, die Suppe, das Brötchen.
cards.lead: You now know the object. On this card: food words with der, die and das, so you learn the article together with every food word you use.

deeper.text: Put food words into three columns in your notebook, one for der, one for die, one for das. The gender often has no logic, but some endings help. Many nouns that end in -e, like Banane and Suppe, are die-words. It is a clue, not a law, so always check each word.

cards.title: Ask: Was isst du? Was trinkst du?
cards.body: was means what. A W-question: was is part 1, the verb is part 2. The answer is the object: the thing you eat or drink. You already know isst and trinkst.

examples.why: The answer is the object: Saft.

steps: Was trinkst du?
Ich trinke Saft.
Was isst Ben?
Ben isst Suppe.
cards.more: was is the key that opens the object. When you ask Was isst du?, you want to hear a food word. Step 1: put was first. Step 2: put the verb second, in the right form for the person. Step 3: add the person. The answer starts with Ich and ends with the thing. Extra example: Was trinkt Ben? – Ben trinkt Milch.
cards.lead: You can name food and drink. On this card: the questions Was isst du? and Was trinkst du?, so you can ask a friend what they eat or drink and answer them.

deeper.text: Notice that the verb form follows the person you ask about. Was isst Ben? has isst, because Ben is the same as er. And Was trinkst du? has trinkst, because of du. You do not choose the form freely. The person decides it, and the question word changes nothing.

cards.title: essen and trinken: all the forms
cards.body: essen changes for du and er/sie: isst. The other forms are regular. trinken is regular. Both verbs can have an object.
cards.more: You know this from chapter 2. essen has one little change: the e becomes i, but only for du and er/sie. Think of two kids who stand out in a row. Step 1: find the person. Step 2: ich, wir, ihr, sie keep the e: esse, essen, esst. Step 3: du and er/sie say isst. trinken has no surprise: trinke, trinkst, trinkt. Extra example: Ihr esst Käse.
cards.lead: You have already seen isst and trinkst in questions. On this card: all six forms of essen and trinken, including the one irregular form, so you can talk about yourself and other people.

deeper.text: Why does du isst look so short? The stem already ends in s, so the du ending is only -t, not -st. It would be issst otherwise. That is why du isst and er isst look identical. Only ihr esst is different, because it has the e again.

cards.title: gern + object
cards.body: gern comes after the verb and the person. Then comes the object. Ich esse gern Suppe. For a yes/no question the verb goes first: Isst du gern Salat?

examples.why: gern after verb + person, then the object.

examples.en: Do you like to eat salad?
examples.why: Verb first, then du, then gern.

cards.more: Think of gern as a small heart you stick on the verb. English needs a whole extra verb: I like to eat. German keeps its normal verb and just adds gern after the verb and the person. So the sentence stays short. Step 1: build the plain sentence: Ben trinkt Milch. Step 2: put gern after trinkt: Ben trinkt gern Milch. Step 3: in a question, the verb comes first and gern still follows the person: Trinkst du gern Milch? Extra example: Wir essen gern Salat.
cards.lead: This is the last card of the lesson. On this card: gern placed after the verb and the person, so you can say what you like to eat or drink.

deeper.text: gern never has an ending and no gender, so it never changes. English says I like eating soup. German does not use a word for like here. It puts gern next to the verb: Ich esse gern Suppe. Think of gern as a small flag that says I enjoy this.

Do you like to eat salad?

lessons.title: Only the masculine changes: der → den, ein → einen
lessons.goal: Say what you eat with der, ein and kein, and know which words change.

grammar.point: The object form is the accusative. Only masculine words change: der → den, ein → einen, kein → keinen. die, das and eine/ein stay.
grammar.oneLine: Ich esse den Apfel. der becomes den, because Apfel is masculine and it is the object.

mistake.why: Apfel is masculine and it is the object. der becomes den.

terms.meaning: the subject form of a noun: der, die, das as you know them
the object form of a noun: only the masculine changes, der → den
a der word, like der Apfel

cards.title: Before we start: the thing that gets eaten
cards.body: Ich esse den Apfel: the word der changes to den. Why? Because the apple is the thing being eaten. Good news: only the masculine words change, and only a little.
steps: You already know: ein, eine, kein, keine from chapter 3
New today: einen and keinen for masculine words
By the end you can: say Ich esse einen Apfel and Ich esse keinen Fisch

examples.why: New today: ein becomes einen, because I eat it.

cards.more: Imagine masculine words get a small badge when they are the thing being eaten: der becomes den, ein becomes einen, kein becomes keinen. All three badges end in -n, so it is easy to spot. The die-words and das-words keep their usual article. So you only watch out for masculine words. You will learn it one word at a time in the next cards.

cards.title: Subject or object? Most words do not change
cards.body: A noun can be the subject (who does it) or the object (what gets it). With die and das nothing changes. Die Katze trinkt die Milch: die comes twice and stays die.

examples.why: Both are feminine: die stays die.
Both are neuter: das stays das.

cards.more: Think of a hotel guest list. A woman can be the guest who orders, or the person the waiter brings to the table. Her name does not change. die and das are like that name: they look the same whether they are the subject or the object. So with die and das, the article gives you no clue. You use the meaning and the word order instead. Step 1: find the verb. Step 2: who does it? Step 3: what gets it? Extra example: Die Frau isst das Brötchen.
cards.lead: Lesson 1 taught you the object. On this card: how to tell the subject from the object, and which words stay the same in both places, so you know where to look for a change.

deeper.text: How do you know who is the subject? Look at who does the verb. With die and das the article cannot tell you, so you use meaning: a woman can eat soup, but soup cannot eat a woman. Only masculine words show the difference in the article, as you will see on the next card.

cards.title: Masculine: der becomes den
cards.body: Only masculine words change. When the masculine noun is the object, der becomes den. The noun itself stays the same. This object form is called the accusative.
cards.more: English shows this change only in small words like he and him: He sees the dog, the dog sees him. German does it with masculine articles: der for the one who acts, den for the thing that gets it. So den is a little like him for things. Step 1: is the noun masculine? Check the der. Step 2: is it the object, the thing eaten or drunk? Step 3: if both are yes, say den. Extra example: Leon trinkt den Kaffee. Kaffee is masculine and gets drunk.
cards.lead: You saw that most words stay the same. On this card: the one masculine change you need for a noun that is the object, so you can spot it in a sentence.

deeper.text: Think of den as der with a small push at the end. German marks the object with a little flag, and for masculine words that flag is the -n. It is easy to spot because it is only one small group of words. The noun itself, like Apfel, does not change.

cards.title: ein becomes einen
cards.body: ein, eine, ein means a or an. For a masculine object ein becomes einen. eine (feminine) and ein (neuter) stay the same.
cards.more: Picture three boxes on a shelf: masculine, feminine, neuter. When a word becomes the object, only the masculine box gets a sticker with -en: ein becomes einen. The other two boxes stay exactly as they were. So you do not need a new rule for eine or ein. Step 1: know the gender. Step 2: masculine object? Add -en to ein. Step 3: feminine or neuter? Do nothing. Extra example: Mira kauft einen Apfel, eine Banane und ein Ei.
cards.lead: Now you can change der to den. On this card: the same kind of change for ein, which becomes einen for a masculine object, so you can say a masculine thing you eat.

deeper.text: With einen, the n is not the only ending you will meet. In speech, Germans often shorten einen to so it sounds like nen: Ich nehme nen Kaffee. That is spoken style only. In writing and in this course, always use the full form einen. And ein before a vowel never changes its sound: ein Ei, ein Apfel.

cards.title: kein becomes keinen
cards.body: kein means no or not a. It follows ein: kein, keine, kein. For a masculine object kein becomes keinen. keine and kein do not change.
cards.more: kein is the no-version of ein. In English you often need two words: not a, or no. German has one word that does both. It takes the same endings as ein, so you already know them all. Step 1: say the sentence with ein: Ich habe einen Löffel. Step 2: put k in front: Ich habe keinen Löffel. Step 3: check that feminine and neuter stay the same: keine Milch, kein Ei. Extra example: Ben trinkt keinen Saft. Saft is masculine, so keinen.
cards.lead: You can now say a or an for a masculine object. On this card: the matching change for kein, so you can say you eat no fish or drink no milk.

deeper.text: Now you can see the whole family: den, einen, keinen. All three end in -n for a masculine object. Do not mix up kein and nicht: kein goes with a noun (kein Fisch), and nicht goes with a verb or an adjective (Ich esse nicht, Die Suppe ist nicht heiß). If you could say ein before the noun, use kein.

example.de: Ich esse keinen Fisch, und die Suppe ist nicht heiß.
example.en: I eat no fish, and the soup is not hot.

cards.title: Two masculine words in one sentence
cards.body: The article shows who is who. The masculine subject keeps der. The masculine object gets den. Der Hund isst den Fisch: the dog eats the fish, not the other way round.

examples.why: der Mann does it, den Kaffee gets it.
der Freund does it, den Kuchen gets it.

steps: Der Hund isst den Fisch.
der Hund = who eats (subject)
den Fisch = what is eaten (object)
cards.more: Imagine two masculine words and no extra clue. In English you use word order: the dog eats the fish. In German the little article tells you, so der means the one who does it and den means the one who gets it. Step 1: look for den. Step 2: den is the object. Step 3: der is the subject. Extra example: Der Junge isst den Salat.
cards.lead: You know how each masculine article changes. On this card: how to tell who does the action when two masculine words sit in one sentence, so you do not mix them up.

deeper.text: Because den marks the object, German can move it to the front. Den Fisch isst der Hund still means the dog eats the fish. The verb stays in part 2, and the articles tell you who does what. English cannot do this: the fish eats the dog is a new story. Germans put the object first to stress it.

cards.title: Spot it in 3 steps
cards.body: Use these 3 steps for every sentence. Do not change die, das or the plural. Change only a masculine object.

examples.de: Ben isst den Joghurt. Er ist lecker.
examples.en: Ben eats the yoghurt. It is tasty.

steps: Find the verb and the subject.
Ask: what gets eaten or drunk? That is the object.
Masculine object? der → den, ein → einen, kein → keinen.
Feminine or neuter? Change nothing.
cards.more: Make it a tiny checklist you say in your head. One: which word is the verb? Two: what does the verb work on? That is the object. Three: is the object masculine? If yes, der becomes den, ein becomes einen, kein becomes keinen. If not, leave it alone. Most words stay the same. Only one group changes. Extra example: Ich esse die Tomate. No change at all.
cards.lead: This is the last card of the lesson. On this card: a three-step check for any sentence, so you can find the object and change only the masculine word.

deeper.text: Step 2 is the key step. Ask what gets eaten, not who eats. The answer is the object. Many learners change every article, but that is wrong: die Wurst stays die Wurst, and das Wasser stays das Wasser. Check the gender first, and change only when the object is masculine.

lessons.title: The full accusative table and verbs with an object
lessons.goal: Use the whole accusative table and know which verbs take an object.

grammar.point: Only masculine changes in the accusative: den, einen, keinen. essen, trinken, kaufen, brauchen and haben take an object. sein does not.
grammar.oneLine: Ich habe einen Hund. But: Das ist ein Hund.

mistake.why: sein has no object, so nothing changes after ist.

terms.meaning: the thing a verb works on: another word for object
the form for many things: die Äpfel
how to think of sein: both sides are the same thing

cards.title: Before we start: the whole table
cards.body: You now know that masculine words change when they are the thing you eat. Today you see the whole table at once, and you learn that other verbs, like kaufen and haben, work the same way.
steps: You already know: Ich esse den Apfel from the last lesson
New today: other verbs with an object, and the one verb that has none, sein
By the end you can: say Ich habe einen Hund

examples.why: New today: haben takes an object too, so einen.
Contrast: sein has no object, so ein stays ein.

cards.more: Think of a toolbox. You already own the einen and den tool. Now you learn it works with more verbs: buy, need, have. The rule never changes. There is just one exception: sein is like an equals sign, so nothing is acted on and nothing changes. You will fill the table step by step, one small card at a time.

cards.title: The full table: der, die, das, plural
cards.body: Here is the whole picture. Only one box changes: masculine. der → den, ein → einen, kein → keinen. All other boxes are the same for subject and object.
cards.more: Think of a grid with 4 columns: masculine, feminine, neuter, plural. In the subject row and in the object row the grid is the same, except for one box. That one box is masculine. So you only have to remember one change: der to den. Step 1: find the gender column. Step 2: look at the object row. Extra example: Ich esse einen Joghurt.
cards.lead: Lesson 2 covered the masculine change. On this card: the whole picture for all genders and the plural in the object position, so you can see what changes and what stays.

deeper.text: Look at what the table really shows: a lot of sameness. Three of the four columns never change, so you do not have many new things to learn. Just remember one small corner, the masculine object. That is the only box where you must stop and think before you speak.

cards.title: Plural objects: nothing changes
cards.body: A plural object never changes. The is die. There is no word for a in the plural, so you say nothing. no is keine. Ich esse Äpfel = I eat apples.

examples.why: plural without article: just the noun.

cards.more: In the singular you can say ein Apfel, one apple. In the plural there is no one, so there is no ein. You just say the noun: Äpfel. It is like English: an apple, but just apples. For no, you take keine. Step 1: plural? Step 2: no article, or die, or keine. Nothing changes between subject and object. Extra example: Ich esse keine Eier.
cards.lead: You have seen the full table. On this card: how plural objects work, with no word for a and keine for no, so you can talk about several things at once.

deeper.text: Plural food words are very common: Äpfel, Eier, Bananen. Notice that Äpfel gets an Umlaut in the plural. A plural with no article means some or in general. English does the same: I eat apples, with no word before it. German leaves it out just as English does.

cards.title: More verbs with an object
cards.body: Many verbs take an object. You know essen and trinken. New: kaufen (to buy) and brauchen (to need). The rule is the same: masculine objects change.
cards.more: A verb with an object is like a hungry mouth: it wants something to bite. essen eats, kaufen buys, brauchen needs. Each of these needs an object. Step 1: spot the verb. Step 2: ask what? Step 3: if that thing is masculine, change the article. These new verbs are regular: ich kaufe, du kaufst, er kauft. Extra example: Anna braucht eine Tasse.
cards.lead: You know essen and trinken take an object. On this card: two new verbs, kaufen and brauchen, so you can say what you buy and what you need.

deeper.text: kaufen and brauchen are both regular, so they follow the endings you know: ich kaufe, du kaufst, er kauft. Notice that you often need something you do not have yet. So the object after brauchen is often something that is still missing, like a spoon or an apple.

cards.title: haben also takes an object
cards.body: haben (to have) is followed by an object too. What you have is the object. Masculine: einen or keinen. Hunger is masculine: Ich habe keinen Hunger = I am not hungry.
cards.more: haben is the same as a person holding something in their hands. What they hold is the object. Ich habe einen Hund: I hold a dog on a lead. For things you have not got, use kein: Ich habe keine Katze. You know Hunger and Durst from chapter 2. Hunger is masculine, so it becomes keinen. Step 1: haben. Step 2: what do you have? Step 3: change only masculine.
cards.lead: You now know several verbs that take an object. On this card: haben, which takes one too, so you can say what you have or do not have, like hunger.

deeper.text: English says I am hungry. German says Ich habe Hunger, which is literally I have hunger. That is why Hunger is an object and takes einen or keinen. Durst (thirst) works the same way and is also masculine. You will often hear it in real life when someone offers food.

cards.title: sein is different: no object
cards.body: sein does not take an object. After ist the noun is just a name for the subject, so nothing changes. Das ist ein Hund. But: Ich habe einen Hund.
cards.more: Imagine sein as an equals sign: Das = ein Hund. Both sides are the same thing, so nothing gets carried over. That is why there is no change. Verbs like essen or haben are arrows: Ich → einen Hund. The thing on the arrow's tip changes. Step 1: sein? No change. Step 2: any other verb with a thing? Change the masculine. Extra example: Der Käse ist gut. (no object)
cards.lead: You can say what you have now. On this card: why sein does not take an object, so you know when the article after ist must stay the same.

deeper.text: Here is a test. Can you put an equals sign in place of the verb? Das = ein Hund. If yes, it is sein, and nothing changes. With haben, one thing owns another, so the second one is an object. So ein Apfel stays ein after ist, but Ich esse einen Apfel needs einen.

cards.title: Ask and answer with an object
cards.body: A yes/no question starts with the verb: Hast du einen Apfel? Answer with ja or nein and a full sentence. For no, use keinen, keine or kein.
steps: Hast du einen Apfel?
Ja, ich habe einen Apfel.
Nein, ich habe keinen Apfel.
cards.more: This is a little game of ask and answer. The question starts with the verb. The answer says ja or nein and then repeats the thing. For no, you swap ein for kein, and the masculine ending stays: einen becomes keinen. Step 1: Hast du einen Apfel? Step 2: Ja, ich habe einen Apfel. Step 3: Or: Nein, ich habe keinen Apfel. Extra example: Isst du den Käse? – Ja, ich esse den Käse.
cards.lead: This is the last card of the lesson. On this card: yes/no questions with an object, answered with ja or nein and keinen, so you can ask someone if they have something.

deeper.text: A yes/no question starts with the verb. Notice hast, from haben, because du is the subject. In the reply you repeat the object with the same ending. For several things you need no article at all, so you can simply ask about the plural. The answer can use keine for no.

lessons.title: möchten: I would like
lessons.goal: Say what you would like, ask others and order politely.

grammar.point: möchten (would like) is the polite want. What you would like is the object: ich möchte einen Kaffee. A second verb goes to the end.
grammar.oneLine: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. Was möchtest du?

mistake.why: The second verb goes to the end of the sentence.

terms.meaning: the polite way to say what you would like
the basic form of a verb: essen, trinken
an infinitive that goes to the end after möchten

cards.title: Before we start: saying what you would like
cards.body: In a café you do not say I want, you say I would like. It sounds nice and polite. Today you learn möchten, the word you need to order a coffee.
steps: You already know: Ich esse einen Apfel with einen from the last lessons
New today: möchten, I would like
By the end you can: say Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte

examples.why: New today: möchte works the same way, so einen.
New today: möchtest du, the question for a friend.

cards.more: Möchten is a polite way to say what you want. Imagine you are at a café counter. You point at the coffee: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. What you would like is the object, so the einen rule you just learned still works. It is a verb like the others, with only small new forms. You will learn it in small steps in the next cards.

cards.title: möchten: I would like
cards.body: möchten means would like. It is the polite way to say what you want. It is irregular: ich and er/sie have the same form, möchte. Learn the six forms.
cards.more: In English, I want a coffee sounds a bit pushy. I would like a coffee is nicer. German has the same two levels. möchten is the nice one. You use it in cafés and shops. Step 1: learn ich möchte. Step 2: add -st for du and -t for ihr. Step 3: wir, sie and Sie say möchten. Extra example: Du möchtest Suppe.
cards.lead: You can use the object with essen and haben. On this card: möchten, the polite way to say would like, and its six forms, so you can say what you want.

deeper.text: How do you make the ö? Say e as in bed, keep your tongue there, and round your lips as for o. That is ö. Without the dots the word changes: mochte, with a plain o, is the past form, meaning liked. So the dots are not decoration. möchte with ö is the polite would like you need in shops.

cards.title: möchten + object
cards.body: What you would like is the object. The accusative rule is the same: masculine einen, feminine eine, neuter ein. Plural: no article.
cards.more: Imagine the café menu as a list of objects. Whatever you point at is the thing you would like, so it is the object, and the gender rule from the last lessons works again. Nothing new to learn, only to use. Step 1: pick the thing: Kaffee. Step 2: say its gender: der Kaffee. Step 3: masculine, so einen: Ich möchte einen Kaffee. Feminine or neuter? eine or ein. Plural? No article: Ich möchte Brötchen. Extra example: Leon möchte einen Salat und eine Suppe.
cards.lead: You know the six forms of möchten. On this card: how the object after möchten follows the article change you already know, so you can order a drink or a snack.

deeper.text: möchten does the same job as haben or essen: it has an object, and masculine objects change. So you do not learn a new rule here, you use the one you already know. That is the good thing about the accusative: one rule works with many verbs, and it keeps coming back.

cards.title: Ask: Was möchtest du?
cards.body: Was möchtest du? asks what you would like. For a yes/no question the verb goes first: Möchtest du einen Tee? Answer with a full sentence.

examples.en: No, I would not like tea.

steps: Was möchtest du?
Ich möchte einen Tee.
Möchtest du einen Kuchen?
Nein, ich möchte keinen Kuchen.
cards.more: This is a small chat between friends. Question one asks what. Question two asks yes or no. Step 1: Was möchtest du? Step 2: answer with Ich möchte and the thing. Step 3: Möchtest du einen Tee? is a yes/no question, so the verb goes first. A no uses kein: keinen Tee. Extra example: Möchtest du einen Kuchen? – Nein, ich möchte keinen Kuchen.
cards.lead: You can say what you would like. On this card: asking someone what they would like, and a yes/no question with möchten, so you can offer things to a friend.

deeper.text: Notice the change from möchte to möchtest: the du form adds -st, but for er/sie, like Ben, the form is möchte. Ask a friend with du and a stranger with Sie. Möchtest du …? is also the friendly way to offer something to a friend, so you will use it all the time.

cards.title: Order politely: bitte
cards.body: bitte means please. Put it at the end: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. In a café (das Café) you can say it short: just the object and bitte. The masculine still says einen.

examples.en: I would like a coffee, please.

cards.more: At a café the waiter is busy. People often say only what they want, plus bitte. That is a very short sentence: no I, no verb. The thing you want is still the object, so the masculine article still changes: Einen Tee, not Ein Tee. Step 1: pick the thing. Step 2: say its article. Step 3: add bitte. Extra example: Eine Suppe, bitte.
cards.lead: You can ask and answer. On this card: adding bitte to make an order polite, and the short version you can use at a café counter.

deeper.text: Germans also order with nehmen: Ich nehme einen Kaffee, I will have a coffee. And in some places you hear Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee, another very polite order. You do not need to build hätte yet, just recognise it. All three forms take the object, so the masculine einen stays.

cards.title: A second verb goes to the end
cards.body: möchten can work with another verb. möchten is part 2. The other verb stays in its infinitive form and goes to the very end. Ich möchte Suppe essen.

examples.en: I would like to eat soup today.
examples.why: möchte is part 2, essen is at the end.

examples.en: What would you like to drink?
Mira would like to buy an apple.

cards.more: Imagine a bracket. möchte holds the front door in chair number 2, and the second verb holds the back door at the very end. The object sits in the middle. Step 1: möchte in part 2. Step 2: put the object next. Step 3: put the infinitive (essen, trinken, kaufen) last. Never put it right behind möchte. Extra example: Wir möchten Tee trinken.
cards.lead: You can order politely now. On this card: how a second verb goes to the very end after möchten, so you can say what you would like to do or eat.

deeper.text: Often the second verb is left out when it is clear: Ich möchte einen Kaffee needs no trinken, because everyone knows what you do with coffee. You add the second verb when the action matters, for example kaufen or essen. And if you use nicht, it sits just before the end verb: Ich möchte heute nicht kochen.

example.en: I would not like to cook today.

cards.title: Polite: Was möchten Sie?
cards.body: To a stranger or a waiter you say Sie. Sie takes möchten. The waiter asks: Was möchten Sie? You answer with ich möchte.

examples.en: I would like a juice, please.

steps: Was möchten Sie?
Ich möchte einen Saft, bitte.
Möchten Sie auch einen Kuchen?
Nein, danke.
cards.more: Think of du and Sie as two doors into the same room. Friends use the du door: Was möchtest du? A waiter, a seller or a teacher like Frau Weber uses the Sie door: Was möchten Sie? Behind the Sie door the verb always looks like the wir form: möchten. Step 1: who are you talking to? Step 2: a stranger or a teacher? Use Sie and möchten. Step 3: answer for yourself with ich möchte. Extra example: Herr Ali, möchten Sie einen Tee?
cards.lead: This is the last card of the lesson. On this card: the polite Sie form of möchten, as a waiter would ask it, so you can answer a question in a shop or café.

deeper.text: Sie takes the same form as wir: möchten. Notice the capital S for the polite Sie, and the small s for she or they. In speech you cannot hear the capital, so the situation tells you. A waiter talking to you means polite Sie, and the verb is then always möchten.

lessons.title: mögen, gern, lieber: what you like
lessons.goal: Say what you like, do not like and prefer; describe food with adjectives.

grammar.point: mögen (to like) is irregular: ich mag, du magst, er mag, wir mögen. Its object follows the accusative rule. Dislikes: nicht gern, keinen. lieber = prefer.
grammar.oneLine: Ich mag Käse. Ich esse nicht gern Fisch. Ich trinke lieber Tee.

mistake.why: mögen already means like. Do not add gern.

terms.meaning: to like a thing or a person
a word that says what something is like: heiß, süß
what you like more: lieber

cards.title: Before we start: saying what you like
cards.body: Do you like cheese? Fish? Today you say what you like, what you do not like and what you prefer. It is a pattern for talking about your own taste.
steps: You already know: Ich möchte einen Kaffee from the last lesson
New today: mögen (to like), nicht gern and lieber
By the end you can: say Ich mag Käse and Ich trinke lieber Tee

examples.why: New today: mögen says what you like in general.

cards.more: Think of a taste scale. Möchten is today, right now: I would like this coffee. Mögen is your general taste: I like coffee. Gern and lieber move your sentence up or down the scale. Gern means like to, lieber means prefer. You already know the object and the verb in part 2. Everything else is built one small piece at a time.

cards.title: mögen: to like
cards.body: mögen means to like a thing or a person. It is irregular: ich mag, du magst, er/sie mag. The umlaut is gone in the singular. In the plural it comes back: wir mögen.
cards.more: English like never changes much: I like, he likes. German mögen has a moody vowel. In the singular it is a plain a: ich mag, du magst, er mag. In the plural the ö comes back: wir mögen, ihr mögt, sie mögen. Picture the ö going home for the plural party. Step 1: singular? Use mag. Step 2: du adds -st. Step 3: plural and Sie keep ö. Extra example: Ihr mögt Kuchen, aber Leon mag Obst.
cards.lead: You know möchten for what you want now. On this card: mögen, which means to like something in general, and its forms, so you can say what you like.

deeper.text: Look at the vowel jump: mag in the singular, mögen in the plural. The Umlaut disappears for ich, du and er. That is just how this verb works, so learn it as a set. Also, ich mag and er mag have no ending at all. You can use mögen for people too, not only food.

cards.title: mögen + object
cards.body: What you like is the object. The accusative rule is the same: masculine changes (der → den). Use it with the or with no article.
cards.more: mögen is like essen: it needs a thing to like. That thing is the object. So the gender rule works here too. Step 1: what do you like? Step 2: masculine? der becomes den. Step 3: feminine, neuter, plural? No change. With no article you mean it in general: Ich mag Käse means I like cheese, any cheese. Extra example: Anna mag den Kaffee.
cards.lead: You have the forms of mögen. On this card: mögen with an object and the same article change, so you can say you like the salad or the soup.

deeper.text: With the or with no article, the meaning is a little different. Ich mag den Käse points to this cheese. Ich mag Käse means cheese in general. The masculine change is the same as with every verb that has an object. So the rule you learned keeps working for you here.

cards.title: mögen or gern?
cards.body: Two ways to say the same thing. Ich mag Käse = Ich esse gern Käse. gern goes with another verb. mögen goes straight to the thing. Keep them apart.

examples.why: Same as: Ben trinkt gern Milch.

cards.more: Two roads, one town. Road one: mögen plus the thing. Road two: another verb plus gern. Both arrive at: I like it. Do not drive on both roads at the same time: Ich mag gern Käse is a traffic jam. Step 1: choose a road. Step 2: build the sentence. Extra example: Ich trinke gern Tee = Ich mag Tee.
cards.lead: You can say what you like. On this card: two ways to say the same thing, one with mögen and one with gern, in two different sentence shapes, so you do not mix them up.

deeper.text: Learners often say Ich mag gern Käse. That is wrong: mögen already means like, so gern is not needed. In real talk you will hear one extra pattern: Ich mag Käse sehr gern, with sehr gern at the end, meaning I like it a lot. For now, keep the two roads apart: mögen plus a thing, or another verb plus gern.

cards.title: What you do not like: nicht gern, kein
cards.body: nicht gern means not like to. nicht comes before gern. After mögen use kein to say you do not like a thing: Ich mag keinen Fisch. Learn nicht gern as one piece.

examples.en: I do not like to eat fish.
Ben does not like to drink milk.

cards.more: Picture a volume knob for liking. gern is up, nicht gern is down. nicht sits right in front of gern, like a little no-sign. For mögen you do not use gern. You say kein, and the masculine word gets keinen. Step 1: choose the verb. Step 2: add nicht gern, or use mögen plus kein. Extra example: Mira mag keine Wurst.
cards.lead: You know two ways to say you like something. On this card: how to say you do not like something, with nicht gern or keinen, so you can turn food down.

deeper.text: Why keinen after mögen but nicht gern after an action verb? Because gern belongs to the verb, and kein belongs to the thing. So ask yourself: do I name a thing right after mögen? Then use kein. Do I have an action verb? Then use nicht gern. That makes the choice clear.

example.en: Anna does not like eating salad.

cards.title: lieber: I prefer
cards.body: lieber means rather or prefer. It sits like gern: after the verb and the person. Ich trinke lieber Tee = I prefer to drink tea. Ask: Was trinkst du lieber?

examples.en: What do you prefer to drink?

cards.more: Picture a ladder with two steps. On step one you say gern: I like it. On step two you say lieber: I like it more. Both sit in exactly the same seat, right behind the verb and the person. To compare two things, say the first with gern and the second with lieber, joined by aber. Step 1: Ich trinke gern Kaffee. Step 2: swap in lieber for the winner: Ich trinke lieber Tee. Extra example: Ben isst gern Fisch, aber er isst lieber Käse.
cards.lead: You can say what you do not like. On this card: lieber, which says you prefer one thing, placed the same way as gern, so you can compare two drinks or foods.

deeper.text: lieber is the comparing form of gern, a bit like English rather. gern says you like it, and lieber says you like it more. It is the first time you meet a word that compares. For now, use it in the same place as gern, and name the thing you prefer.

cards.title: möchten or mögen?
cards.body: möchten is for now: what you would like at this moment. mögen is for always: what you like in general. Ich möchte einen Tee = now. Ich mag Tee = in general.

examples.de: Mira mag Käse, aber heute möchte sie Suppe.
examples.en: Mira likes cheese, but today she would like soup.

cards.more: Imagine your fridge and today's order. The fridge is full of what you like in general: Ich mag Käse. Today's order is one thing for right now: Heute möchte ich eine Suppe. Both verbs look similar, but they answer different questions. Step 1: is it about always? Use mögen, often with no article. Step 2: is it about now? Use möchten, often with einen, eine or ein. Extra example: Leon mag Kaffee, aber jetzt möchte er einen Tee.
cards.lead: You know both words now. On this card: when to use möchten for right now and mögen for always, so you pick the right one for each sentence.

deeper.text: Think of möchten as a moment and mögen as a character trait. Ich möchte einen Tee means I want one right now. Ich mag Tee means I always like it. A waiter asks with möchten, and a friend asks about your taste with mögen. You use both every day.

cards.title: Say what it is like: sein + adjective
cards.body: An adjective says what something is like. After ist it has no ending: Die Suppe ist heiß. Put nicht before it to say not: Die Suppe ist nicht heiß.
cards.more: An adjective is a label you stick on the thing. Hot, cold, sweet, spicy. After ist the label stays plain, with no ending at all. English does the same: The soup is hot. Step 1: name the thing with its article: der Kaffee. Step 2: add ist. Step 3: add the label: heiß. For a no, put nicht just before the label. For a lot, put sehr before it. Extra example: Der Kuchen ist sehr süß, aber der Kaffee ist nicht heiß.
cards.lead: This is the last card of the lesson. On this card: sein with describing words about food, like hot and cold, so you can say what a food is like.

deeper.text: zu is a warning word: Die Suppe ist zu heiß means it is too hot to eat, so it is a problem. sehr only makes it stronger: sehr heiß is very hot, which can be fine. Germans also say lecker for tasty food, and it is a very common word at the table. These small words stand before the adjective and never change.

lessons.title: Quantities and prices
lessons.goal: Say how much you want, ask the price and say prices.

grammar.point: After a quantity the food has no article: ein Kilo Äpfel. The quantity word follows the accusative rule (einen Liter). Was kostet …? asks the price.
grammar.oneLine: Ich möchte ein Kilo Äpfel. Was kostet der Käse? Zwei Euro fünfzig.

mistake.wrong: Ich möchte ein Kilo die Äpfel.
mistake.why: After a quantity word the food has no article.

terms.meaning: how much: ein Kilo, eine Flasche
the measure word: Kilo, Liter, Packung
what something costs: 2,50 €

cards.title: Before we start: how much, how many, how much it costs
cards.body: At the market you want a kilo of apples and you need to know the price. Today you say how much you want and ask Was kostet …?
steps: You already know: Ich kaufe einen Apfel from chapter 4
New today: a quantity word, like ein Kilo, and the price question
By the end you can: say Ich kaufe ein Kilo Äpfel and ask Was kostet der Käse?

examples.en: I buy a kilo of apples.
examples.why: New today: ein Kilo, and no article before the food.
New today: kosten asks the price.

cards.more: Imagine a shopping bag. You say how much goes in, a kilo, a litre, a pack, and then what it is. The quantity word comes first, and the food follows with no little word before it. Ein Kilo Äpfel, not ein Kilo die Äpfel. And the price is an easy question: Was kostet …? You will practise this step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: Quantities: how much?
cards.body: To buy food you say how much. Learn these quantity words with their articles: das Kilo, das Gramm, der Liter, die Flasche, die Packung, das Stück. The food comes right after.

examples.en: I buy a kilo of apples.
Ben would like a litre of milk.
Mira buys a bottle of water.

cards.more: A quantity word is like a measuring cup. First you say the cup, then what is in it. In English you use of: a kilo of apples. German leaves of out. You just say the cup, then the food. Step 1: pick the cup (Kilo, Liter, Flasche). Step 2: say the food right after it. Extra example: Ich möchte eine Packung Reis.
cards.lead: Lesson 5 was about what you like. On this card: quantity words like a kilo, a litre and a bottle, placed before the food, so you can say how much you buy.

deeper.text: English says a kilo of apples. German leaves out of and just puts the two words next to each other: ein Kilo Äpfel. The quantity comes first, then the food. Notice that you never say a word for of here. It is simpler than English, so you can say it quickly.

example.en: Ben needs a bottle of milk.

cards.title: No article after the quantity
cards.body: After a quantity you do not use der, die, das or ein. You say the food on its own. ein Kilo Äpfel, not ein Kilo die Äpfel. Use die only when you name one special thing.

examples.en: We need a packet of rice.
I would like a piece of cake.

cards.more: Think of a full cup. You never say the cup of the coffee. You say a cup of coffee. German is the same: the food after a quantity has no article, no der, no ein. It is easy: say less. Step 1: say the quantity. Step 2: say the food, bare. Extra example: eine Flasche Saft, not eine Flasche den Saft.
cards.lead: You know the quantity words. On this card: why the food after a quantity has no article, so you can say the food on its own.

deeper.text: Why no article? The food is only an amount, not a particular thing. English works the same way: a kilo of apples, not a kilo of the apples. Only when you point to a special thing do you add der, die or das. For general amounts, say the food on its own.

example.en: We buy a kilo of cheese.

cards.title: The quantity word follows the accusative rule
cards.body: The quantity word is the object, so its article follows the rule. Only the masculine one changes: der Liter becomes einen Liter. das Kilo stays ein Kilo. die Flasche stays eine Flasche. The food does not matter.

examples.en: I would like a litre of milk.
examples.why: Liter is masculine: einen. Milch does not matter.

examples.en: I would like a kilo of cheese.
examples.why: Kilo is neuter: ein. Käse is masculine, but it does not matter.

examples.en: I would like a bottle of juice.

cards.more: Watch the quantity word, not the food. Milch is feminine, but you say einen Liter Milch. Why? Because the word right after ein is Liter, and Liter is masculine. The food comes later and has no article, so its gender does not matter here. Step 1: look at the unit. Step 2: its gender decides. Extra example: Ich kaufe einen Liter Saft.
cards.lead: You can say no article after a quantity. On this card: how the quantity word itself takes the right article for the object, so you can get einen Liter or ein Kilo right.

deeper.text: Unlike English two kilos, German says zwei Kilo, with no plural ending, and the same for Liter, Gramm and Stück. But real containers can be counted, so they take a normal plural: zwei Flaschen, drei Packungen. Die-words that end in -e or -ung almost always add -n or -en in the plural, so Tasse becomes Tassen.

example.de: Ich kaufe zwei Kilo Äpfel und drei Flaschen Wasser.
example.en: I buy two kilos of apples and three bottles of water.

cards.title: More than one: zwei Kilo, zwei Flaschen
cards.body: After a number, Kilo, Gramm, Liter and Stück stay the same. The feminine words Flasche and Packung add -n. zwei Kilo, drei Liter, aber zwei Flaschen, zwei Packungen.

examples.en: I would like two kilos of apples.
Ben buys three bottles of water.
We need two packets of rice.

cards.more: Picture the shopping bag again. Some measuring words are like a scale: Kilo, Gramm, Liter, Stück. A number in front does not change them: zwei Kilo, drei Liter, zwei Stück. English adds -s: two kilos, three litres. German does not. The containers are different: you can count bottles and packets, so they take a plural: zwei Flaschen, drei Packungen. Step 1: say the number. Step 2: unit or container? Step 3: only the container gets -n. Extra example: zwei Packungen Reis.
cards.lead: You know the accusative for quantities. On this card: how numbers change the quantity words, with an -n for some of them, so you can buy two or three of something.

deeper.text: After a number, Kilo and Liter stay singular, a bit like English two kilo. Feminine words add -n or -en: Flasche becomes Flaschen, Packung becomes Packungen. Gender knowledge helps here: die words that end in -e or -ung almost always add -n or -en in the plural.

example.en: We buy three litres of juice.

cards.title: Ask the price: Was kostet …?
cards.body: Was kostet …? and Wie viel kostet …? both ask the price (der Preis). kostet for one thing, kosten for more than one. The thing is the subject, so der stays der: Was kostet der Käse?

examples.why: der stays: the cheese is the subject.

examples.en: How much does the milk cost?

cards.more: A price question is about the thing, not about you. The thing is the star, the subject, so it keeps der. It is not an object like in Ich esse den Käse. Step 1: ask Was kostet or Wie viel kostet. Step 2: say the thing with der, die or das. Step 3: one thing? kostet. Many things? kosten. Extra example: Was kostet das Brötchen?
cards.lead: You can say how much you buy. On this card: asking the price with Was kostet and Wie viel kostet, and the change for many things, so you can ask what something costs.

deeper.text: At the till the seller tells you the total with machen: Das macht drei Euro fünfzig. That means: that comes to 3,50 euros. You can also ask Was macht das? for the total. And Wie teuer ist der Käse? asks how expensive the cheese is. Answer every price question with the thing as the subject and kostet or macht.

example.en: That comes to three euros fifty.

cards.title: Say the price: Euro and Cent
cards.body: Prices have a comma: 2,50 €. Say Euro first, then Cent: zwei Euro fünfzig. Under one euro, say only Cent: 0,80 € is achtzig Cent. Euro and Cent never add -s.

examples.de: Der Käse kostet zwei Euro fünfzig.
Ein Liter Milch kostet zwei Euro.
examples.en: A litre of milk costs two euros.

cards.more: You know your numbers from chapter 2. A price is just two numbers with a word in the middle. 3,40 € is three euros, forty: drei Euro vierzig. Under one euro you skip the euros: 0,70 € is siebzig Cent. And do not add -s: zwei Euro, not zwei Euros. Step 1: say the euros. Step 2: say the cents. Extra example: 4,20 € = vier Euro zwanzig.
cards.lead: This is the last card of the lesson. On this card: how to say prices in euros and cents, so you can pay for food at a market.

deeper.text: In writing, 2,50 € uses a comma where English uses a point. It is the other way round from English. In shops people often drop the words and say zwei fünfzig. In this course you say Euro and Cent in full. Notice that Cent never gets an -s.

Under one euro, say only Cent.

lessons.title: Shopping: shops, nehmen and the shop talk
lessons.goal: Name the shops, take what you want and manage a short shopping talk.

grammar.point: Learn the shop words and where you buy as pieces (im Supermarkt). nehmen (to take) and haben take an object. The shop talk uses fixed phrases.
grammar.oneLine: Ich nehme den Käse. Haben Sie Brötchen? Das ist alles, danke.

mistake.why: ich takes -e. Only du and er/sie say nimm-.

terms.meaning: a group of words you learn as one piece, like in der Bäckerei
a list of what you need: quantity + food
the person who sells things

cards.title: Before we start: shopping
cards.body: You are at the shop, and the seller asks: Was darf es sein? What do you say? Today you learn the shops, the verb nehmen and the little phrases of a shop talk.
steps: You already know: Ich möchte ein Kilo Äpfel from the last lesson
New today: nehmen (to take) and the shop phrases
By the end you can: say Ich nehme den Käse and ask Haben Sie Brötchen?

examples.en: I would like a kilo of apples.

examples.why: New today: nehmen takes an object, so den.
New today: a polite question for the seller.

cards.more: Think of a short play with two parts: the seller and you. The seller has little fixed lines, like Was darf es sein?, and you have yours: Ich nehme …, Das ist alles, danke. You do not build the lines, you learn them as ready-made pieces, like song lines. Then you fill in what you buy. We will go step by step through the whole talk in the next cards.

cards.title: Shops: where do you buy what?
cards.body: Learn four shop words with their articles. die Bäckerei sells bread and rolls. die Metzgerei sells meat and sausage. der Supermarkt sells everything. der Markt sells fresh food.
cards.more: Each shop is like a little room with its own things. The bakery has bread and rolls, the butcher has meat and sausage, the supermarket has a bit of everything, and the market has fresh food. Step 1: say the shop with its article. Step 2: think of one thing you can buy there. Extra example: Die Metzgerei hat Wurst.
cards.lead: You can ask prices now. On this card: four shop words with their articles and what each one sells, so you know where to buy bread, meat or milk.

deeper.text: Bäckerei and Metzgerei both end in -ei, and nouns that end in -ei are die-words. That is a safe clue for you at this level. Metzgerei is common in the south and west. In some northern places you will hear Fleischerei for the same shop. Both are die-words.

cards.title: Where you buy: learn these pieces
cards.body: To say where you buy, learn these as whole pieces: im Supermarkt, in der Bäckerei, in der Metzgerei, auf dem Markt. Why it is im, der and dem comes in a later chapter. For now copy them.

examples.de: Ich kaufe Brötchen in der Bäckerei.
examples.en: I buy rolls in the bakery.

examples.de: Mira kauft Äpfel auf dem Markt.
examples.en: Mira buys apples at the market.
Ben buys cheese in the supermarket.

cards.more: You do not take a clock apart to read the time. Do the same here. Do not take in der Bäckerei apart. Learn it like a single long word. Why der and not die? Later chapter. Step 1: say the whole piece out loud, three times. Step 2: put it at the end of the sentence, after the object. Extra example: Anna kauft Wurst in der Metzgerei.
cards.lead: You know the shop words. On this card: where-you-buy phrases learned as whole pieces, so you can say where you shop.

deeper.text: This is the same idea as with the months: in dem becomes im. In der stays in der. auf dem Markt means at the market, because you stand on the market square. Learn each one as a whole piece, with its little words. The reason for dem and der comes later.

example.de: Anna kauft Brot in der Bäckerei.
example.en: Anna buys bread in the bakery.

cards.title: nehmen: I will take it
cards.body: nehmen means to take. In a shop you say it when you decide: Ich nehme den Käse. It is irregular: du nimmst, er nimmt. The object follows the accusative rule.

examples.why: ich nehme. Käse is masculine: den.

cards.more: Imagine pointing at the cheese counter and deciding. In English you say I will take the cheese. German uses the present: Ich nehme den Käse. No will needed. nehmen is a little odd in the du and er/sie forms: the e turns into i and the h turns into mm: du nimmst, er nimmt. Step 1: ich, wir, ihr, sie keep neh-. Step 2: du and er/sie use nimm-. Step 3: the thing you take is the object. Extra example: Ben nimmt einen Saft.
cards.lead: You can say where you buy things. On this card: nehmen, which means to take and which you use when you decide to buy, with its irregular forms.

deeper.text: In a shop or a café, Ich nehme … is the normal way to decide, not rude at all. German uses the present tense for a decision you make right now, where English says I will take or I'll have. So Ich nehme die Suppe is a full order. Friends also ask Was nimmst du? when they look at a menu together.

example.de: Was nimmst du? – Ich nehme die Suppe.
example.en: What are you having? – I will have the soup.

cards.title: The shop talk: Was darf es sein?
cards.body: Learn the shop talk as pieces. The seller asks Was darf es sein? (What would you like?) and later Sonst noch etwas? (Anything else?). You end with Das ist alles, danke.
steps: Was darf es sein?
Ich möchte ein Kilo Äpfel, bitte.
Hier, bitte. Sonst noch etwas?
Ja, ich nehme auch 200 Gramm Käse.
Hier, bitte. Sonst noch etwas?
Nein, das ist alles, danke.
cards.more: A shop talk is like a dance with fixed steps. The seller leads: Was darf es sein? You answer with Ich möchte and the thing. The seller asks: Sonst noch etwas? You can say Ja, ich nehme… or Das ist alles, danke. Learn the three phrases by heart. They never change. Step 1: Was darf es sein? Step 2: you order. Step 3: Sonst noch etwas? Step 4: Das ist alles, danke.
cards.lead: You can decide what to take. On this card: the seller's phrases for asking what you want and whether you need anything else, so you can follow a whole shop talk.

deeper.text: Was darf es sein? is literally What may it be? The word darf comes from a verb you do not need yet. Here it is simply a polite shop phrase. Sonst noch etwas? means anything else. Learn these as set phrases, like Can I help you? in English. You do not need to analyse them.

example.en: I will take two rolls, please.

cards.title: Ask: Haben Sie …?
cards.body: Ask if the shop has something: Haben Sie Brötchen? What they have is the object, so the usual rule works: einen, eine, ein. In the answer you can say wir (the shop).
cards.more: You already know Haben Sie…? from chapter 2: it is a yes/no question, so the verb goes first. In a shop it asks: have you got this? The thing is the object, so a masculine word still says einen. The seller often answers with wir, meaning the whole shop. Step 1: Haben Sie … Step 2: add the thing. Extra example: Haben Sie Milch?
cards.lead: You know the shop talk. On this card: asking if a shop has something, and how to answer with wir haben, so you can check what is in stock before you buy.

deeper.text: Haben Sie …? uses the Sie form of haben. In the answer the shop speaks as wir, because a shop is a group of people. For several things you need no article: Haben Sie Äpfel? For one thing, the same rule as always works: einen, eine, ein. Nothing new here.

cards.title: The shopping list
cards.body: A shopping list (die Liste) has no full sentences. Write the quantity and the food: 1 Kilo Äpfel, 1 Liter Milch. No articles. To say it, begin: Ich brauche …

examples.de: Ich brauche ein Kilo Äpfel, einen Liter Milch und eine Packung Reis.
examples.en: I need a kilo of apples, a litre of milk and a packet of rice.
examples.why: Quantity + food, no article after it.

cards.more: A list is like a short text message to yourself. You skip all the extra words: no I, no verb. Only the quantity and the thing. To read it out loud you add: Ich brauche. Objects go in a row, joined by und. Step 1: write the list with quantities. Step 2: say Ich brauche before it. Step 3: use und before the last item. Extra example: Ich brauche Käse und Brot.
cards.lead: This is the last card of the lesson. On this card: how to write a shopping list and say what you need with Ich brauche, so you can plan a shop before you go.

deeper.text: A list is only a group of nouns, so it has no verb. When you say it aloud, you add Ich brauche, and the accusative comes back. ein Kilo Äpfel stays ein, but einen Liter Milch needs the -en. So read the list, then fit the article endings as you speak.

example.en: I need a litre of juice.

lessons.title: Meals and time first: zum Frühstück, morgens
lessons.goal: Name your meals, say what you eat when and put the time first.

grammar.point: A time word can start the sentence. The verb stays in part 2: Zum Frühstück esse ich ein Brötchen. morgens, mittags, abends, heute and zum Frühstück are time words.
grammar.oneLine: Morgens trinke ich Kaffee. Zum Frühstück esse ich ein Brötchen.

mistake.why: The verb stays in part 2. The subject goes after it.

terms.meaning: breakfast, lunch or dinner
a word that says when: heute, morgens, am Montag
the first part of the sentence: it can be a time word

cards.title: Before we start: meals and time first
cards.body: When do you eat? What do you eat for breakfast? Today you talk about your meals and your day, and you put the time at the start of the sentence.
steps: You already know: Am Montag spiele ich Tennis from chapter 2
New today: zum Frühstück and morgens at the start
By the end you can: say Zum Frühstück esse ich ein Brötchen

examples.de: Zum Frühstück esse ich ein Brötchen.
examples.en: For breakfast I eat a roll.
examples.why: New today: zum Frühstück starts the sentence.

examples.en: In the morning I drink coffee.
examples.why: New today: morgens is a time word too.

cards.more: Imagine your day as a row of boxes: morning, noon, evening. You name a box first, then say what happens in it. German lets you put that time first, but the verb keeps its seat in part 2, just like with am Montag. So the person, ich, hops behind the verb. You will see it in small steps, one meal at a time, in the next cards.

cards.title: Three meals
cards.body: Germans have three meals. das Frühstück is breakfast. das Mittagessen is lunch. das Abendessen is dinner. All three are neuter, so they use das.
cards.more: Think of a German day as three plates on a table. The morning plate is das Frühstück: rolls, butter, coffee. The noon plate is das Mittagessen. The evening plate is das Abendessen. For many Germans the evening plate is cold: bread, cheese and sausage, often called Abendbrot. Step 1: learn the three words with das. Step 2: link each to its time of day. Step 3: name one typical food for each. Extra example: Zum Abendessen esse ich Brot und Käse.
cards.lead: You can talk about shopping now. On this card: the three meals of the day, all of them das-words, so you can name breakfast, lunch and dinner.

deeper.text: Mittagessen is a compound: Mittag (noon) plus Essen (food). Abendessen is Abend plus Essen. German builds long words from short ones, and the last part decides the gender. Essen is a das-word, so the whole word is das. Frühstück is its own word, and it is also das.

cards.title: zum Frühstück: for breakfast
cards.body: Say what you eat for a meal with zum: zum Frühstück, zum Mittagessen, zum Abendessen. Learn each one as one piece. Why it is zum comes in a later chapter. It goes before the object.

examples.de: Ich esse zum Frühstück ein Brötchen.
examples.en: I eat a roll for breakfast.

cards.more: In English you say for breakfast, for lunch, for dinner. German uses zum in the same place: zum Frühstück, zum Mittagessen, zum Abendessen. Do not swap it for für, because für Frühstück sounds wrong. Picture zum as a small label you glue to the meal. Step 1: say the verb and the person. Step 2: add the zum piece. Step 3: add what you eat. Or start with the zum piece and put the verb second. Extra example: Ben trinkt zum Abendessen Tee.
cards.lead: You know the three meals. On this card: how to say what you eat for a meal, with zum before the meal, so you can name food for each one.

deeper.text: zum is zu and dem squeezed together, just like im. Das Frühstück is a das-word, so zu dem becomes zum. In English you say for breakfast. German chooses zu instead of for. Notice that zum comes before the meal and that the meal never changes.

cards.title: morgens, mittags, abends
cards.body: These words say when, again and again. morgens = in the morning, mittags = at noon, abends = in the evening. They have a small s at the end. They sit like time words.

examples.en: I drink coffee in the morning.
We eat bread in the evening.

cards.more: These three little words are clocks that tick every day. morgens is every morning, mittags is every noon, abends is every evening. All three end in s. You do not need am or zum. Step 1: choose the time word. Step 2: put it after the verb and the person, or at the start. Extra example: Mira isst abends Salat. heute means today.
cards.lead: You can say what you eat at each meal. On this card: time-of-day words that mean every morning, every noon and every evening, so you can say when you do things.

deeper.text: morgens, mittags and abends are small adverbs, so they have no gender. The -s is a small old ending that means regularly: morgens means every morning. Compare heute, which means today only. Notice that morgens has a small m. The noun der Morgen has a capital.

example.en: Anna drinks water in the evening.

cards.title: Start with the time: the verb stays second
cards.body: Put the time word first and the verb stays in part 2. The subject now follows the verb. The object stays after it. Same words, new order.

examples.de: Zum Frühstück esse ich ein Brötchen.
examples.en: For breakfast I eat a roll.
examples.why: time first, verb second, then ich.

examples.en: In the morning I drink coffee.
examples.why: morgens first, then trinke, then ich.
heute first, then esse, then ich.

cards.more: You know this from the days of the week. Think of chairs again. Chair 1 can be the subject or a time. Chair 2 is for the verb, always. If chair 1 is a time, the subject moves to chair 3. The meaning does not change. The object goes at the end. Step 1: put the time on chair 1. Step 2: verb on chair 2. Step 3: subject on chair 3. Step 4: object last. Extra example: Abends isst Ben Suppe.
cards.lead: You can say when something happens. On this card: putting the time word first, with the subject moving after the verb, so the word order still works.

deeper.text: Always check part 2: whatever comes first, the verb stays second. A common mistake is Morgens ich trinke Kaffee. It is wrong, because the verb must be in part 2. This rule works for every statement and every W-question. If the time comes first, the subject goes behind the verb.

example.en: In the evening Ben eats soup.

cards.title: Ask: Was isst du zum Frühstück?
cards.body: Ask what someone eats and when. Was isst du zum Frühstück? Was trinkst du morgens? Ask Wann frühstückst du? for the time. Answer with the time word.

examples.en: What do you eat for breakfast?
What do you drink in the morning?

steps: Was isst du zum Frühstück?
Zum Frühstück esse ich ein Brötchen.
Was trinkst du morgens?
Morgens trinke ich Kaffee.
cards.more: A good way to learn is to ask and answer. The question word starts: was or wann. The verb is part 2. The person comes next. The time word comes last, after the person. In the answer you can put the time first: Zum Frühstück esse ich Müsli. Step 1: ask. Step 2: answer with ich. Extra example: Wann frühstückst du? – Am Sonntag.
cards.lead: You can put the time first. On this card: asking what someone eats and when they eat it, so you can ask a friend about their day.

deeper.text: You can make a verb from the noun Frühstück: frühstücken, to have breakfast. It is a regular verb: ich frühstücke, du frühstückst. It needs no object. For lunch and dinner there is no such verb, so Germans say zu Mittag essen and zu Abend essen. Wann frühstückst du? asks the time, and the answer usually starts with the time word.

example.en: I have breakfast in the morning.

cards.title: immer and oft: how often
cards.body: immer = always and oft = often. They sit after the verb and the person, like gern. With a time word first: Morgens trinke ich immer Kaffee.

examples.en: In the morning I always eat fruit.
examples.why: time first, then verb, ich, immer.

cards.more: immer and oft are like gern: little words that sit right behind the verb and the person. They tell you how often. immer is a full circle, oft is a half circle. Step 1: write the plain sentence: Ich trinke Kaffee. Step 2: slide immer after trinke and ich. Step 3: you can also start with morgens. Extra example: Anna isst oft Obst.
cards.lead: This is the last card of the lesson. On this card: immer for always and oft for often, placed after the verb and the person, so you can say how often you eat something.

deeper.text: immer and oft sit in the same place as gern: after the verb and the person. German has more words for this idea, like manchmal (sometimes) and nie (never), and they sit in the same place. You will learn them later, but the position will already feel natural to you.

lessons.title: Offering, accepting, declining, and ä ö ü
lessons.goal: Offer food, say yes or no politely, enjoy a meal and say ä, ö and ü.

grammar.point: Offer with a yes/no question (Möchtest du einen Kaffee?). Accept with Ja, gern or Ja, bitte. Refuse with Nein, danke. Noch einen Kaffee? offers more.
grammar.oneLine: Möchtest du einen Tee? – Ja, bitte. / Nein, danke. Ich bin satt.

mistake.right: Möchtest du einen Tee? – Ja, bitte.
mistake.why: danke alone often means no, thanks. For yes say Ja, bitte or Ja, gern.

terms.meaning: to ask someone if they want something
to say yes to an offer
to say no to an offer politely

cards.title: Before we start: offering and saying yes or no
cards.body: A friend offers you cake. You want to say yes, or you are full and want to say no, politely. Today you learn the kind little phrases of a meal, and the sounds ä, ö and ü.
steps: You already know: Möchtest du einen Tee? from the last lessons
New today: Ja, gern. Ja, bitte. Nein, danke.
By the end you can: offer food and answer politely

examples.why: New today: a short, friendly yes.
New today: a short, polite no.

cards.more: Think of a table with friends. Someone holds out the plate and asks the question you already know. You answer with two little words, like a smile in words: Ja, gern. Or: Nein, danke. That is all you need to be polite at any German table. You also practise three new sounds, ä, ö and ü, step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: Offer food and drink
cards.body: To offer something, ask a yes/no question: the verb goes first. Möchtest du einen Kaffee? Use möchten with du, Sie or ihr. nehmen works too: Nimmst du Zucker? What you offer is the object.

examples.en: Would you like a piece of cake?
Would you like to try it?

rows: a guest (der Gast) at a party (die Party)

cards.more: Imagine you hold a plate and hold it out to someone. In German you ask a yes/no question with the verb first. Pick the right person: du for a friend, Sie for a stranger, ihr for two friends. What you offer is the thing at the end, an object, so masculine words say einen. Step 1: verb first. Step 2: person. Step 3: the thing. Extra example: Möchtet ihr einen Tee?
cards.lead: You can name meals now. On this card: how to offer food with a yes/no question, using möchten or nehmen, so you can ask a friend or a stranger if they want something.

deeper.text: Möchtest du …? and Nimmst du …? both offer something. möchten sounds a little more careful, and nehmen sounds more direct. The verb comes first in both. Notice that the thing you offer takes the masculine ending einen. Zucker (sugar) has no article here, so it does not change.

cards.title: Say yes: Ja, gern. Ja, bitte.
cards.body: To accept, say Ja, gern. (yes, with pleasure) or Ja, bitte. (yes, please). Both sound friendly. You can add a full sentence: Ja, ich nehme einen Kaffee.

examples.en: Yes, I will have a coffee.

steps: Möchtest du einen Tee?
Ja, gern.
Möchtest du ein Stück Kuchen?
Ja, bitte.
cards.more: Think of two doors that open for yes. Door one: Ja, gern. It means yes, I would love that. Door two: Ja, bitte. It means yes, please. Both are fine. If you want more, add a sentence with nehmen: Ja, ich nehme einen Kaffee. Step 1: choose gern or bitte. Step 2: stop here, or add a sentence. Extra example: Ja, gern. Ich nehme ein Stück.
cards.lead: You can offer things. On this card: two friendly ways to say yes, so you can accept an offer and sound warm.

deeper.text: Ja, gern means yes, with pleasure, so you really want it. Ja, bitte is simply yes, please. Both are warm. Notice that gern now stands alone, with no verb. You used it after a verb before, but it can also answer a question by itself. You can add a full sentence after it.

example.de: Ja, bitte, ich möchte einen Saft.
example.en: Yes, please, I would like a juice.

cards.title: Say no: Nein, danke.
cards.body: To refuse politely, say Nein, danke. You can add a reason. Careful: danke alone often means no, thanks! For yes, say Ja, bitte or Ja, gern.

examples.de: Nein, danke. Ich habe keinen Hunger.
examples.en: No, thanks. I am not hungry.

cards.more: In English you can say Thanks for yes and for no. In German this is risky. Offered a tea, if you just say Danke, many people hear no. So choose: Ja, bitte for yes, Nein, danke for no. To be extra kind, give a short reason. Step 1: Nein, danke. Step 2: Ich habe keinen Hunger. or Ich mag keinen Fisch. or Ich bin satt.
cards.lead: You can say yes now. On this card: a polite no with danke and a short reason, so you can refuse food without sounding rude.

deeper.text: Be careful: danke alone can mean no, thanks, when you decline something. Many learners say Danke and then get food they did not want. A short reason makes your no soft and friendly. For example, satt means full after eating, and Ich habe keinen Durst is a clear reason too.

example.de: Nein, danke, ich habe keinen Durst.
example.en: No, thanks, I am not thirsty.

cards.title: More? Noch einen Kaffee?
cards.body: To offer more, say noch (another, more) and the thing. Often there is no verb: Noch einen Kaffee? The masculine still says einen. You can answer Ja, bitte. or Nein, danke.
cards.more: At a table the host does not talk much. Noch einen Kaffee? is a short, warm question. There is no verb because you can see what is meant. But the grammar is still there: a masculine thing gets einen. Step 1: say noch. Step 2: say the article. Step 3: say the thing. Answer with Ja, bitte. or Nein, danke. Ich bin satt. Extra example: Noch einen Tee?
cards.lead: You can accept and refuse. On this card: offering more with noch, and the article changes you already know, so you can offer a second coffee or roll.

deeper.text: noch means more or another. Noch einen Kaffee? is a question with no verb, because everyone can see what you are offering. Notice that the masculine einen stays, because it is still an object, even without a verb. For feminine and neuter words nothing changes: noch eine Suppe, noch ein Brötchen.

cards.title: The sounds ä, ö, ü
cards.body: Three letters have two dots: ä, ö, ü. ä sounds like e in bed. ö: say e, but round your lips. ü: say ee, but round your lips. The dots matter: Apfel is one apple, Äpfel is many.

examples.en: I would like cheese and apples.
examples.why: ä in Käse, Äpfel. ö in möchte.

cards.more: Your mouth has to learn new shapes. Step 1 for ä: open your mouth a little and say e, as in bed. Step 2 for ö: say e, then push your lips forward into a small circle. Step 3 for ü: say ee, then push your lips into the same small circle. Practise with food words: Käse, Brötchen, Küche. Listen to a video for the exact sounds. Extra example: Frühstück has ü.
cards.lead: You can offer more food now. On this card: the letters with two dots, ä, ö and ü, and how each one sounds, so you can say words like Käse and Küche clearly.

deeper.text: ä, ö and ü are separate letters, not just a, o and u with decoration. They can change the meaning of a word: schon means already, but schön means nice. If you cannot type the dots, you may see ae, oe and ue in writing, but that is only a keyboard trick. Always say the real sound.

cards.title: At the table: Guten Appetit!
cards.body: Before a meal Germans say Guten Appetit! The answer is Danke, gleichfalls! (thanks, the same to you). When you drink together, you say Prost! Saying these is polite.
cards.more: Meals have little rituals. Before you start, someone says Guten Appetit! You smile and say Danke, gleichfalls! It is like saying: and you too! When you lift a glass, everybody says Prost! If a host offers more, you can say Ja, bitte or Nein, danke. Ich bin satt. Step 1: wait for Guten Appetit. Step 2: answer it. Step 3: enjoy.
cards.lead: This is the last card of the lesson. On this card: what to say before a meal, what to answer, and what to say when you drink together, so you can join in at a table.

deeper.text: gleichfalls means the same to you, and it works for other good wishes too, not only meals. Prost is said while you look at the other person and clink glasses. Germans find that eye contact important and polite. A name at the end, like Anna, makes it more personal and friendly.

reading.text:
Mira: Hallo, Ben! Am Sonntag essen wir zusammen. Was brauchen wir?

Ben: Gut! Ich esse gern Käse und Schinken. Ich kaufe den Käse und den Schinken.
Mira: Ich esse keinen Schinken, und ich esse keine Wurst. Ich esse Tomaten und Eier.
Ben: Hast du einen Teller? Ich habe keinen Teller.
Mira: Ja, ich habe zwei Teller und einen Löffel.
Ben: Super! Was trinkst du?
Mira: Ich trinke Kaffee. Du trinkst Tee, ja? Und Anna trinkt Saft.
Ben: Ja! Ich kaufe den Saft.
